passage:
"Payal, it's midnight. What are all these boxes?"
"Old textbooks, Ma. Forty-three so far."
Vandana stepped over one. "Placements start next month. You should be practising interviews."
"I am. Ten to twelve every morning." Payal wrote First Year Physics on a box. "This is for after."
"After what?"
"After I graduate. Juniors who can't buy books will borrow these free. The college gave me a shelf in the library."
"With your name on it?"
"No name. Just a register." Payal shrugged. "When I'm gone, it'll still be there. Some girl from a village might pass physics because of a book I carried up three floors. I like that."
Vandana was quiet. Then she picked up the marker. "Your handwriting is terrible. Give me that."

qa.q: How many old textbooks had Payal collected so far?
qa.a: Forty-three so far.

qa.q: Why doesn't Payal want her name on the shelf?
qa.a: She isn't doing it for credit; she wants the library to outlast her and help juniors, and that thought pleases her.

qa.q: How does Payal balance the book project with her ambition?
qa.a: She practises interviews from ten to twelve every morning and works on the boxes at night, so the project sits alongside her placement goals.

qa.q: What does Vandana picking up the marker suggest about how she now sees the project?
qa.a: She seems to accept and even support it, moving from worry about placements to quietly helping 😊

grounding: A young woman builds a free textbook library for juniors, not for credit but to leave something that lasts, alongside preparing for placements.

passage: When I started going to the government school on Saturdays last year, I told people it was for my CV. That wasn't true, but it was easier to say. I, Siddharth, spend the other six days chasing a good rank for my master's, and I want that badly. My mother jokes that her son collects projects like stamps. But on Saturdays I sat with eight kids and a box of scrap motors, and we built a fan that barely turned. Pradeep, the quietest one, fixed the wiring before I did. This March I graduate and move away. So I spent December writing a simple guide in Hindi and English, with drawings, and trained Pradeep and another boy to run the club. Nobody there will remember my name in five years. I hope they're still building fans.

qa.q: What did Siddharth and the kids build first?
qa.a: A fan that barely turned, from a box of scrap motors.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth tell people the Saturdays were for the CV?
qa.a: He probably felt a bit shy admitting he simply cared; "for my CV" was easier to say than wanting something to outlast him.

qa.q: What choice in December helps the club outlast Siddharth?
qa.a: Writing a simple guide in two languages and training Pradeep and another boy to run the club after he leaves.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel being trusted to run the club?
qa.a: He may feel proud and more confident, since his skill at fixing the wiring was clearly noticed.

grounding: A young man mentors schoolchildren and makes sure the club outlasts him, while still chasing his own ambitions.

passage:
Volunteer coordinator's note, Green Lane Tree Trust. Sarika.
Lavanya (19) has come every second Sunday since June, even in her exam month. Today she stayed back after planting to paint small wooden labels for the sixty saplings, with the tree name and the date and no volunteer names. When I suggested she add hers to the board, she laughed and said, "The trees will be here after I'm gone. That's enough." She also mentioned she's applying for a research internship in Bengaluru and asked if I would write a reference. I said yes gladly. Next: I'll pair her with two new school volunteers so she can show them the watering schedule, and I'll send the reference by Friday.

qa.q: What did Lavanya paint on the labels?
qa.a: The tree name and the date, with no volunteer names.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's laugh and "That's enough" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She seems content, even happy, that her effort will outlast her; the trees lasting matters more to her than her name on the board.

qa.q: How does Lavanya show that giving back can sit alongside ambition?
qa.a: She keeps coming every second Sunday while also applying for a research internship and asking for a reference.

qa.q: Why might Sarika pair Lavanya with new school volunteers?
qa.a: Sarika sees Lavanya's commitment and wants it passed on, so the care continues even when volunteers change.

grounding: A young volunteer plants and labels trees without seeking credit, wanting her effort to outlast her, while also pursuing an internship.

passage:
Thursday, 11:30 pm
Finally tested the tank alarm at the primary school in Kunal's village. When the water runs low, a buzzer goes off and a red light blinks in the headmistress's room. Before this, the kids found out the tank was empty when the taps coughed at lunch.
Kunal soldered, I wrote the code on my old laptop, total cost less than a pair of shoes. No marks, no certificate, not going on my CV. Mummy asked why I spend Sundays on it with exams coming.
Honest answer: I want something I made to still be working after I'm gone. In five years some kid will wash their hands and never know my name, and I like that.
Also: entrance mock tomorrow at seven, and I still want that top institute seat badly. Both things are true.
Bhavna

qa.q: What happens when the school tank's water runs low?
qa.a: A buzzer goes off and a red light blinks in the headmistress's room.

qa.q: Why does Bhavna like that some kid will never know Bhavna's name?
qa.a: Bhavna feels content being unknown, wanting the tank alarm to outlast its maker rather than to earn credit.

qa.q: How does Bhavna hold the tank project and ambition together?
qa.a: Bhavna works on the alarm on Sundays but still sits the entrance mock and wants the seat badly, keeping both.

qa.q: How might the headmistress see the red light blinking in the office?
qa.a: The headmistress might see it as a small, lasting help that spares the children dry taps at lunch.

grounding: A young adult builds a tank alarm for a village school not for credit but so the effort outlasts them, alongside ongoing ambition.

Wasim: you missed the fest again
Suraj: was in Rahimpur. recording Hafiz chacha at the loom
Wasim: the weaving thing? for which subject
Suraj: no subject. just recording the old weavers talking about their patterns before they're gone. 14 so far
Wasim: ok but why. no credits, no internship
Suraj: idk. my nana wove. nobody recorded him
Suraj: I want there to be something in the town library that stays after all of us
Wasim: that's actually nice
Suraj: also still applying for the Bengaluru internship. I'm not a saint 😅
Wasim: noted
Wasim: need someone to hold the mic next time?
Suraj: yes!! sunday 8am

qa.q: How many old weavers has Suraj recorded so far?
qa.a: Fourteen so far.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel about the recordings, and what does Suraj want them to become?
qa.a: Suraj seems to feel a quiet regret that nobody recorded Suraj's own nana, and wants something in the town library that stays after all of them.

qa.q: Why is it healthy that Suraj is still applying for the internship?
qa.a: It shows the project sits beside ambition rather than replacing it, so Suraj isn't choosing between giving back and a career.

qa.q: What changed in Wasim's view during the chat?
qa.a: Wasim moved from asking 'but why' to calling it nice and offering to hold the mic.

grounding: A young adult records old weavers so something lasting stays in the town library, not for credit, while still pursuing an internship.
